props.title: Ghost Ship
props.initialSlug: Salvage crew meets horror aboard haunted luxury liner

sections.content: Ghost Ship (2002) stands as a notable entry in the maritime horror subgenre, following the tradition of Death Ship (1980) and Deep Rising (1998). The film's opening sequence, featuring a gruesome mass-casualty event on a luxury liner, remains one of horror's most memorable cold opens. While the film struggled critically, it exemplifies early 2000s horror's emphasis on elaborate death scenes and gothic atmosphere, similar to other Dark Castle Entertainment productions like House on Haunted Hill (1999) and Thirteen Ghosts (2001).

sections.content: The haunted ship subgenre often serves as a claustrophobic twist on the haunted house formula. Ghost Ship shares DNA with films like Event Horizon (1997), where isolation and inescapable confines amplify the horror. The salvage crew premise echoes DeepStar Six (1989) and Leviathan (1989), where working-class characters confront supernatural or monstrous threats in remote locations.

The film's production design deserves special mention, with the Antonia Graza serving as a character itself. This attention to nautical atmosphere follows a tradition seen in The Fog (1980) and Virus (1999), where maritime settings provide both historical weight and inherent isolation. The film's mix of ghost story and salvage operation narrative would later influence works like Triangle (2009) and Mary (2019). SUBHEAD: Maritime Horror Evolution

sections.content: Ghost Ship marked a transition point between practical effects-driven horror of the 1990s and the increasing CGI reliance of the 2000s. Its influence can be seen in later nautical horror films like Blood Vessel (2019) and Mary (2019), though these later entries often opted for more psychological approaches over spectacle-driven scares.
